verses.html: The lot came out for the children of Joseph from the Jordan at Jericho, at the waters of Jericho on the east, even the wilderness, going up from Jericho through the hill country to Bethel.
It went out from Bethel to Luz1, and passed along to the border of the Archites to Ataroth2;
and it went down westward to the border of the Japhletites, to the border of Beth Horon the lower, and on to Gezer; and ended at the sea.
The children of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, took their inheritance.
This was the border of the children of Ephraim according to their families. The border of their inheritance eastward was Ataroth Addar, to Beth Horon the upper.
The border went out westward at Michmethath on the north. The border turned about eastward to Taanath Shiloh, and passed along it on the east of Janoah.
It went down from Janoah to Ataroth, to Naarah, reached to Jericho, and went out at the Jordan.
From Tappuah the border went along westward to the brook of Kanah3; and ended at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Ephraim according to their families;
together with the cities which were set apart for the children of Ephraim in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Manasseh, all the cities with their villages.
They didn’t drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer; but the Canaanites dwell in the territory of Ephraim to this day, and have become servants to do forced labor.4

footnotes.html: Bethel and Luz (v. 2) are commonly taken as the same place, with Luz the older Canaanite name (Gen 28:19, 35:6) and Bethel the name Jacob gave it. The boundary description here, however, treats them as distinct points (‘from Bethel to Luz’), which may preserve a memory of a twin-site arrangement — the sanctuary on one ridge and the older town on another.

Ataroth (vv. 2, 7) is generally taken as the same place as Ataroth-Addar in v. 5, located at Khirbet ʿAtara south of Bethel. A minority view holds that the simple form in v. 7 names a separate Ataroth in the Jordan valley near Naarah; the pin reuses Ataroth-Addar.

The brook of Kanah (v. 8) is Wadi Qana, draining the central hill country westward through the Sharon Plain to the Mediterranean. It is the natural feature dividing Ephraim’s allotment from Manasseh’s, and reappears as a boundary in 17:9.

Gezer not driven out (v. 10) — a parallel to Judah’s failure at Jerusalem (15:63). Tel Gezer was finally taken by Pharaoh and given to Solomon as a dowry (1 Kgs 9:16); the same pattern of unfinished conquest recurs through the second half of Joshua and the opening of Judges.
